usage: 가방에서 지갑을 꺼냈어요.
I took my wallet out of my bag.
에서 marks the place you take something out of
냉장고에서 반찬 좀 꺼내 줄래?
Can you take the side dishes out of the fridge?
casual 줄래? is how you ask a roommate or partner for a quick favor
examples: 주머니에서 핸드폰 꺼내지 마세요. 영화 시작했어요.
Don't take your phone out of your pocket. The movie started.
common reminder in a theater
에어컨 리모컨 어디 뒀더라, 서랍에서 꺼내 봐.
Where did I put the AC remote, try taking it out of the drawer.
꺼내 봐 = try taking it out and see
택배 박스에서 물건만 꺼내고 박스는 접어서 버려요.
I take only the items out of the delivery box and fold the box to throw away.
everyday routine with online orders
nuance: 꺼내다 is the default verb for taking something out of an enclosed space like a bag, pocket, fridge, or drawer. It contrasts with 빼다 (to pull/remove a fitted thing) — you 꺼내 a wallet from a bag but 빼 a key from a lock. It also means 'to bring up' a topic: 그 얘기 왜 꺼냈어? (Why did you bring that up?).
mistakes: Using 빼다 instead of 꺼내다 for taking things out of a bag — 빼다 implies pulling out something stuck or fitted, not retrieving from open space.

usage: 젓가락으로 반찬을 집어요.
I pick up the side dish with chopsticks.
(으)로 marks the tool you pick something up with
바닥에 떨어진 거 집어 줄 수 있어요?
Can you pick up the thing that fell on the floor?
everyday request when your hands are full
examples: 마트에서 아무거나 집지 말고 유통기한 확인해.
At the store, don't just grab anything — check the expiration date.
집다 here = casually grabbing an item off a shelf
고기 집어 먹을 집게 좀 주세요.
Can I get tongs to pick up the meat?
common at a Korean BBQ place
펜 좀 집어 줄래요? 손이 안 닿아요.
Could you pick up the pen for me? I can't reach it.
집어 주다 = pick up and hand to someone
nuance: 집다 means to pick something up with your fingers, chopsticks, or tongs — a precise grasp of a small object. It differs from 들다 (to lift), which is about raising something with your hand or arm regardless of size. You 집어 a single fry but 들어 a heavy box. Despite ending in ㅂ, 집다 is NOT a ㅂ-irregular verb, so it conjugates 집어요, not 지워요.
mistakes: Conjugating it as a ㅂ-irregular (집어요 is correct, NOT 지워요) — 집다, 잡다, 좁다 all keep the ㅂ.

usage: 택배는 문 앞에 두고 가 주세요.
Please leave the package in front of the door.
두다 = put something somewhere and leave it there
우산 여기 뒀는데 어디 갔지?
I put my umbrella here, where did it go?
common when you can't find something you set down
examples: 지갑을 집에 두고 나왔어요.
I left my wallet at home (and came out).
두고 나오다 = leave behind by mistake, a very frequent phrase
그냥 둬, 내가 나중에 치울게.
Just leave it, I'll clean up later.
그냥 둬 = leave it as is, don't touch it
화분은 햇빛 잘 드는 데 둬요.
Put the plant where the sunlight comes in well.
두다 for deciding a thing's resting spot
nuance: 두다 means to place something somewhere and leave it there — the emphasis is on the resting state, not the motion. 두고 오다/나오다 (to leave something behind) is one of the most useful expressions for residents: 핸드폰 두고 왔어요 (I left my phone behind). Compare with 놓다, which stresses the act of setting down. 두다 is a regular ㅜ-stem verb: 두어요 contracts to 둬요.
mistakes: Forgetting the ㅜ+어 contraction — the polite form is 둬요 (or 두어요), not 두요.

usage: 반찬을 통에 담아요.
I put the side dishes into a container.
에 marks the container you put things into
봉투에 따로 담아 주시겠어요?
Could you put it in a separate bag for me?
polite request you'll use constantly at checkout
examples: 국은 그릇에 담고 밥은 공기에 담아.
Put the soup in a bowl and the rice in a rice bowl.
담다 = transfer food into serving dishes
장바구니에 담아 두고 나중에 결제했어요.
I added it to the cart and paid later.
online shopping: 장바구니에 담다 = add to cart
남은 음식은 반찬통에 담아서 냉장고에 넣어요.
Put the leftover food in a container and into the fridge.
common kitchen instruction
nuance: 담다 specifically means to put or load contents into a container — a bag, bowl, box, or shopping cart. Online, 장바구니에 담다 is the standard phrase for 'add to cart.' It differs from 넣다 (to put in / insert), which is broader and emphasizes the inserting motion; 담다 emphasizes filling a container with contents. 담다 is regular: 담 + 아요 = 담아요.
mistakes: Using 넣다 when ordering takeout — natives say 봉투에 담아 주세요 (put it in a bag), reserving 넣다 for inserting one item into a slot.

usage: 교과서 30쪽 펴세요.
Open your textbook to page 30.
책을 펴다 = open/spread a book, what a teacher says
허리 좀 펴고 앉아.
Sit up straight (straighten your back).
펴다 also means to straighten a bent body part
examples: 이불 펴고 잘 준비해.
Lay out the blanket and get ready to sleep.
이불을 펴다 = spread out bedding on the floor
우산 펴는 버튼이 어디 있지?
Where's the button to open the umbrella?
우산을 펴다 = open an umbrella
구겨진 영수증을 펴서 다시 봤어요.
I unfolded the crumpled receipt and looked again.
펴다 = flatten something wrinkled or folded
nuance: 펴다 is the all-purpose verb for unfolding, spreading out, or straightening — opening a book, laying out bedding, opening an umbrella, or straightening your back. It is the natural opposite of 접다 (to fold). 펴다 is a ㅕ-stem verb, so the past tense contracts: 펴 + 었어요 = 폈어요. Don't confuse it with 펼치다, which is more dramatic ('to unfold widely / unfurl').
mistakes: Writing the past tense as 펴었어요 — the ㅕ+었 always contracts to 폈어요.

usage: 충전 케이블을 단자에 끼워요.
I insert the charging cable into the port.
에 marks the slot you wedge something into
책갈피 좀 끼워 줄래?
Can you slip a bookmark in?
끼우다 = fit something snugly into a gap
examples: 유심을 여기에 끼우면 돼요.
You just insert the SIM card here.
essential when setting up a phone in Korea
문에 발 끼우지 마세요. 다쳐요.
Don't wedge your foot in the door. You'll get hurt.
끼우다 for getting a body part caught/stuck in a gap
손가락에 반지를 끼웠어요.
I put the ring on my finger.
반지를 끼우다/끼다 = put a ring on
nuance: 끼우다 means to insert or wedge something snugly into a slot or gap — a SIM card, a cable, a bookmark, or a ring onto a finger. It implies a tight, fitted placement, unlike 넣다 (general 'put in') or 담다 (fill a container). The plain form 끼다 is also common (반지를 끼다, 안경을 끼다). 끼우다 is a regular ㅜ-stem verb: 끼우 + 어요 = 끼워요.
mistakes: Using 넣다 for a SIM card or cable — natives say 유심을 끼우다 / 케이블을 끼우다 because it's a fitted insertion, not loose dropping-in.

usage: 밥 위에 계란을 얹어요.
I place an egg on top of the rice.
위에 marks the surface you set something on top of
라면에 치즈 한 장 얹어 먹어 봐.
Try eating your ramen with a slice of cheese on top.
common food hack phrasing
examples: 어깨에 손을 살짝 얹었어요.
I lightly placed my hand on his shoulder.
얹다 = rest something lightly on a surface
케이크 위에 딸기를 예쁘게 얹어 주세요.
Please place the strawberries nicely on top of the cake.
request at a bakery
선반에 얹어 놓은 책이 떨어졌어요.
The book I had set on the shelf fell.
얹어 놓다 = leave something resting on top
nuance: 얹다 means to rest or place something lightly on top of a surface — an egg on rice, a hand on a shoulder, a topping on a dish. The key idea is 'on top of,' so it almost always pairs with 위에. It is gentler and more specific than 놓다 (general 'set down') or 두다 (leave somewhere). 얹다 is regular: 얹 + 어요 = 얹어요.
mistakes: Spelling the polite form as 언어요 — keep the ㅈ: 얹어요 (the ㄵ cluster resyllabifies but the spelling stays 얹어요).

usage: 수건으로 머리를 감쌌어요.
I wrapped my hair with a towel.
(으)로 marks what you wrap around something
깨지지 않게 그릇을 뽁뽁이로 감싸 주세요.
Please wrap the dishes in bubble wrap so they don't break.
useful when shipping fragile items
examples: 추워서 담요로 몸을 감싸고 있었어요.
It was cold so I was wrapping myself in a blanket.
감싸다 = wrap around for warmth or protection
손을 따뜻하게 감싸 주는 장갑이에요.
These are gloves that wrap your hands up warmly.
감싸 주다 = wrap up cozily
친구가 무조건 나를 감싸 줬어요.
My friend totally stood up for me no matter what.
나를 감싸 주다 = shield/defend a person; note it's the person, not 편을
nuance: 감싸다 means to wrap something around an object to cover or protect it — a towel around hair, bubble wrap around dishes, a blanket around your body. It carries a nuance of enveloping and protecting, and figuratively means to stand up for or shield a person (나를 감싸 주다). Don't say 편을 감싸다 — for taking someone's side you 편을 들다, but you 감싸다 the person directly. Compare with the basic 싸다 (to wrap/pack); 감싸다 adds the 'around / enveloping' feel. It is a regular ㅏ-stem verb, so 감싸 + 았어요 = 감쌌어요.
mistakes: Writing the past tense as 감싸았어요 — the ㅏ+았 contracts fully to 감쌌어요.

usage: 택배 상자를 뜯었어요.
I tore open the delivery box.
뜯다 = rip open packaging or a sealed item
과자 봉지 좀 뜯어 줄래?
Can you tear open the snack bag?
everyday request, 봉지를 뜯다 = open a bag
examples: 고지서 안 뜯어 봤는데 또 왔네.
I didn't even open the bill and another one came.
뜯어 보다 = open and check (mail/bills)
새 휴대폰 필름 뜯고 바로 새 거 붙였어요.
I peeled off the new phone's film and put a new one on right away.
뜯다 = peel off a protective film
포장 뜯지 말고 그대로 반품하세요.
Don't tear open the packaging — return it as is.
important for returns/exchanges
nuance: 뜯다 means to tear, rip, or peel something open — a delivery box, a snack bag, an envelope, or a protective film. It implies pulling apart a sealed or attached thing, often destructively. Note the difference from 풀다 (to untie/undo, like a knot or ribbon): you 뜯어 sealed tape but 풀어 a tied bow. Despite ending in ㄷ, 뜯다 is NOT a ㄷ-irregular verb, so the polite form stays 뜯어요, never 뜰어요.
mistakes: Treating it as a ㄷ-irregular (it is regular: 뜯어요, never 뜰어요) — unlike 듣다/걷다, the ㄷ does not change to ㄹ.

usage: 코트를 옷걸이에 걸었어요.
I hung my coat on the hanger.
에 marks where you hang something
벽에 액자 좀 걸어 줄 수 있어요?
Can you hang the picture frame on the wall?
common moving-in / decorating request
examples: 수건은 여기 걸어 두면 돼요.
You can just hang the towel here.
걸어 두다 = hang it up and leave it
문에 자물쇠 걸었는지 확인했어요?
Did you check if you put the lock on the door?
걸다 also = fasten/latch a lock
가방을 의자에 걸어 놨어요.
I hung my bag on the chair.
걸어 놓다 = hang and leave hanging
nuance: 걸다 means to hang something on a hook, hanger, wall, or rail — a coat, a towel, a picture frame. It also covers latching a lock (자물쇠를 걸다) and, in a separate common sense, making a phone call (전화를 걸다). The opposite for taking down is 내리다 or 떼다. 걸다 is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㄹ, giving 겁니다 and the future 걸 거예요, while keeping 걸어요 in the present.
mistakes: Saying 걸읍니다 for the formal form — the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다, so it is 겁니다.

usage: 설거지통에 그릇을 쌓아 놨어요.
I stacked the dishes in the sink.
쌓다 = pile things up on top of each other
박스를 너무 높이 쌓지 마세요.
Don't stack the boxes too high.
쌓다 with 높이 = stack high
examples: 책상에 책이 잔뜩 쌓여 있어요.
There's a big pile of books on the desk.
쌓이다 (passive) = be piled up; useful pair
경력을 차근차근 쌓고 있어요.
I'm steadily building up my career.
쌓다 figuratively = accumulate experience/career
눈이 밤새 쌓여서 길이 미끄러워요.
Snow piled up overnight so the roads are slippery.
눈이 쌓이다 = snow accumulates
nuance: 쌓다 means to stack or pile things on top of each other — dishes, boxes, books. It also works figuratively for accumulating something over time: 경력을 쌓다 (build a career), 스트레스가 쌓이다 (stress builds up). The passive form 쌓이다 ('to be piled up / accumulate') is just as common in daily speech. 쌓다 ends in ㅎ but conjugates regularly: 쌓 + 아요 = 쌓아요.
mistakes: Dropping the ㅎ in writing (쌓아요, not 싸아요) — the ㅎ is silent in speech but must stay in spelling.

usage: 손잡이를 꽉 쥐세요.
Grip the handle tightly.
꽉 쥐다 = grip firmly; said on buses/subways
아이가 내 손가락을 꼭 쥐었어요.
The child gripped my finger tightly.
쥐다 = close the hand around something
examples: 펜을 너무 세게 쥐면 손이 아파요.
If you grip the pen too hard your hand hurts.
쥐다 = hold by clenching the fist
주먹을 꽉 쥐고 참았어요.
I clenched my fist and held it in.
주먹을 쥐다 = make a fist
지하철에서 손잡이 잘 쥐고 계세요.
Hold the strap firmly on the subway.
polite safety reminder
nuance: 쥐다 means to grip or clench — to close your hand firmly around something like a handle, a pen, or to make a fist (주먹을 쥐다). It emphasizes the squeezing grasp of the whole hand, unlike 집다 (pick up with fingertips) or 잡다 (catch/hold, broader). 쥐다 is a ㅟ-stem verb: 쥐 + 어요 = 쥐어요 (sometimes spoken as 줘요), and the formal form is 쥡니다.
mistakes: Confusing 쥐다 (grip in the fist) with 집다 (pick up with fingertips) — you 쥐어 a handle but 집어 a coin.
